title: Overhaul electrical system components on agricultural equipment

lessons.title: Preparing to overhaul electrical parts
lessons.html:
Which parts are overhauled?

In the farm workshop you can overhaul some electrical parts instead of buying new ones. The most common are:

  • Starter motor – brushes, bushes, solenoid contacts, drive pinion.
  • Alternator – brushes, bearings, regulator, diodes.
  • Wiring harness sections – damaged wires, plugs and terminals.
  • Light units and switches.

An overhaul can cost far less than a new starter or alternator. But if the main parts like the armature or windings are burnt, a new or exchange unit may be cheaper. Ask your supervisor to decide.

Tools you need

  • multimeter (volts, ohms, continuity);
  • test lamp;
  • soldering iron, heat-shrink tube and crimping tool;
  • bearing puller and soft hammer;
  • fine sandpaper (not emery cloth on a commutator unless the manual says so);
  • the workshop manual with the wear limits.

Safety

  1. Disconnect the battery negative first before removing any electrical part.
  2. Label every wire before you take it off. Take a photo.
  3. Starter motors are heavy. Support them when you remove the last bolt.
  4. A soldering iron is very hot. Put it in its stand, and keep it away from fuel and rags.
  5. Work in fresh air when soldering or using contact cleaner.

lessons.title: Overhauling a starter motor and alternator
lessons.html:
Starter motor

  1. Clean the outside. Mark the end covers and the body so they go back the same way.
  2. Remove the solenoid, end covers and brush holder as the manual shows.
  3. Take out the armature and lay out all parts in order.

Check:

  • Brushes – measure their length. Replace if shorter than the manual limit.
  • Commutator – the copper segments should be smooth and clean. Clean lightly with fine sandpaper. Deep grooves or burnt segments mean the armature needs specialist repair or replacement.
  • Bushes – the shaft must not wobble in them.
  • Drive pinion – teeth must not be chipped. It must turn one way only.
  • Solenoid contacts – burnt contacts cause clicking with no cranking.
  • Armature – use the multimeter to check it is not shorted to the shaft as the manual shows.

Alternator

  • Mark the case halves, then remove the pulley, regulator and brush pack.
  • Check the brushes for length and the slip rings for wear.
  • Turn the bearings by hand. Replace rough or noisy bearings.
  • Test the diodes with the multimeter diode setting, as the manual shows. A diode should pass current one way only.

Fit new brushes, bearings and seals, then reassemble using your marks. Tighten the through-bolts evenly. Turn the shaft by hand to check it is free.

lessons.title: Repairing wiring and testing on the machine
lessons.html:
Repairing a damaged wire

  1. Find the damaged part of the wire. Cut out the bad section.
  2. Use new wire of the same thickness or thicker. A thinner wire can overheat and burn.
  3. Strip the ends, join them with a crimp connector or solder, and cover with heat-shrink tube.
  4. Never just twist wires together and wrap them with tape. That join will fail in the dust and wet.
  5. Tie the wire away from heat and moving parts.

Replacing terminals and plugs

  • Use the right crimp terminal for the wire size.
  • Pull gently on the terminal after crimping to test it.
  • Put a little dielectric grease in plugs on machines that work in wet conditions, if the manual allows.

Testing on the machine

  1. Fit the part and connect the wires using your labels. Reconnect the battery negative last.
  2. Starter: the engine must crank strongly. Check no smoke or burning smell.
  3. Alternator: with the engine running, measure battery voltage. It should be higher than with the engine off but within the manual range. The charge warning light must go out.
  4. Wiring and lights: check every light and gauge on that circuit works.
  5. Check the fuse does not blow and the wires do not get warm.

Write the faults found, parts fitted and test results on the job card.

Key points

  • Disconnect the battery negative first and label every wire.
  • Check brushes, bearings and bushes against the manual limits.
  • Use wire of the same thickness or thicker and seal joins with heat-shrink.
  • Never twist and tape wires as a repair.
  • Test cranking, charging voltage and lights after the overhaul.
